title: 15 Cops Who Turned Out to Be Serial Killers
fullText: Number one, Gerard John Schaefer. The detectives in Martin County, Florida, in the summer of 1972, were faced with a problem that did not fit the usual shape of a crime. Two teenage girls had walked into a police station, badly shaken, and told a story that made no sense on paper. A man in a uniform, a man with a badge, a man who was supposed to protect them, had driven them at gunpoint into a swamp, tied them to trees, and told them what he intended to do. And then, for reasons no one could explain, he had received a phone call, panicked, and let them live. The man they described was not a stranger lurking in the dark. He was a sheriff's deputy. He was one of their own. That contradiction sat at the center of everything that followed, and investigators would spend years trying to understand it. How does a man sworn to enforce the law use the law itself as a hunting tool? To answer that, they had to trace the life of Gerrard John Schaefer. And what they found was a pattern that had been visible for years, if only someone had known where to look. Schaefer was born in March of 1946 in Wisconsin, and raised in a household he later described in bitter terms. By his own accounts given years afterward, he grew up resentful of his father and fixated on his younger sister, whom he believed received the affection he was denied. Whether that resentment explains anything, is a question for psychologists, not detectives, but investigators would later note that the anger he carried toward women, appeared early, and never left. As a young man, he tried and failed at several paths. He studied for the priesthood and abandoned it. He tried teaching and was let go reportedly after unsettling behavior around female students. Each failure, sir, seemed to sharpen something in him rather than soften it. What drew the attention of local law enforcement in hindsight was how badly Schaefer wanted to become law enforcement himself. He joined the Wilton Manners Police Department and was dismissed within months. Then he was hired by the Martin County Sheriff's Office. To the men who worked beside him, he seemed eager, talkative, perhaps a little strange, but nothing that raised alarm. He had passed the hiring process. He wore the uniform. He had authority over exactly the kind of people he had spent his life resenting. Young women alone on Florida's roadsides. And here the investigative timeline and the criminals timeline begin to run side by side. In July of 1972, Schaefer stopped two young women, Nancy Trotter and Paula Wells, on the pretense of official business. He offered them a ride. They accepted because why would you refuse a police officer? He drove them to a remote area, produced a weapon, and bound them. What saved their lives was almost accidental. Schaefer received a radio call, and had to leave, warning them not to move. The moment he was gone, they freed themselves and fled. When they reached the authorities, the description they gave pointed straight at the deputy. Schaefer's own sheriff arrested him. His initial explanation was almost laughable in its inadequacy. He claimed he had only been trying to frighten the girls to teach them a lesson about hitchhiking. He was charged, released on bond, and here the investigation stalled in a way that would haunt everyone involved. Because while he was awaiting the consequences of that first case, Schaefer was not finished. Keep that detail in mind because it becomes far more important later. In September of 1972, two more young women, Susan Place and Georgia Jessup, were last seen leaving a home in the company of a man who called himself Jerry. Months passed with no answers. Susan's mother, however, had done something that would prove decisive. When her daughter left, she had written down a partial description and details of the man, uneasy about him even then. It was the kind of small, ordinary act of caution that changes the direction of an entire case. In April of 1973, human remains were discovered on Hutchinson Island. They were identified as the two missing girls. The investigation that had begun with two survivors now had two victims, and the man at the center of both was already known to police. When detectives searched the room Schaefer kept at his mother's home, they found what would become the backbone of the case against him. Jewelry and personal items belonging to missing and murdered young women and pages of his own violent writings describing the abduction and killing of women in detail that mirrored the real crimes. The evidence chain tightened around him. property linked to victims, the survivor's testimony, and Schaefer's documented pattern of behavior combined into something no jury could dismiss. In 1973, he was convicted of two counts of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Investigators believed he was responsible for many more deaths, and over the years he would boast, taunt, and hint at a body count far higher than two, though much of it could never be proven, and some of it was likely the invention of a man who craved infamy, the near misses in his case, became a lesson taught for decades afterward. The first two survivors had reported him, and yet the window between that report and his final proven murders had stayed open long enough for two more young women to die. Every investigator who studied the file understood the weight of that gap. A badge had granted him trust, and the slow machinery of the system had granted him time. Schaefer never walked free again. In December of 1995, he was killed by another inmate inside a Florida prison. his death as violent as the acts that had put him there. He left behind a mountain of self- mythologizing writing, much of it unreliable, and a genuine question that has never fully closed. How many young women accepted a ride from a uniformed man on a Florida road and were never seen again. The proven cases are terrible enough. The uncertainty around the rest is its own kind of unresolved wound. Number two, Manuel Partardo Jr. When Miami homicide detectives began finding bodies in early 1986, they assumed they were looking at the ordinary bloodshed of the cocaine years. The victims were connected to the drug trade. They had been shot deliberately professionally. It looked like the settling of accounts between criminals, the kind of killing that filled Miami's morgs in that era. What investigators did not yet understand was that the man leaving these bodies was not a rival dealer or a cartel enforcer. He was a former police officer, a decorated one, and he believed he was doing the city a favor. That was the disorienting truth at the heart of the case. The killer thought of himself not as a criminal, but as a cleaner of criminals, and untangling that delusion would take detectives deep into the life of Manuel Partardo Jr., a man who had once stood at the top of his police academy class. Partardo was born in September of 1956. After serving in the Navy, he entered the Florida Highway Patrol Academy and graduated at the very top of his class in 1979. By every early measure, he was a model of what a young officer should be. He was disciplined, ambitious, and outwardly committed to the work. But the arc of his career bent downward through a series of accusations and terminations. He left the highway patrol under a cloud involving falsified traffic tickets. He then joined the Sweetwater Police Department where he built a reputation as aggressive and effective. But that chapter ended in disgrace as well, tied to allegations of misconduct and eventually his involvement in a scheme that saw him traveling out of state in ways that drew the attention of authorities. By the mid 1980s, stripped of his badge and his standing, Partardo had drifted into exactly the world he had once policed. He became involved in cocaine trafficking, and it was inside that world, according to the case built against him, that his self-image curdled into something monstrous. He decided that the drug dealers around him were vermin, that the justice system was too weak to deal with them, and that he was uniquely qualified to render judgment. Over roughly 3 months in 1986, Partardo and an associate committed a string of murders. The victims, nine people in total, including Mario Amador, Roberto Alonso, Luis Robo, Uliano Leo, Michael Miote, Farakinero, Saramusa, Rammon Alvo, and Daisy Ricard, were tied in various ways to drug activity, though not all of them fit the neat category Partardo used to justify his actions. Some were killed over money, over failed deals, over debts. The vigilante story he told himself was investigators came to believe a costume draped over ordinary greed and a growing appetite for killing. The path that led detectives to him ran through the physical evidence and the ordinary friction of a criminal operation. As the bodies accumulated, the connections between victims and a small circle of associates became clearer. When police finally moved on Partardo and searched his belongings, they found something that removed any doubt about his mindset. He had kept records. He had photographs. He had memorabilia connected to his crimes and to a personal ideology that shocked even hardened investigators. This was not a man who had killed in a moment of rage and tried to bury the memory. This was a man who had documented his work and taken pride in it. His arrest turned the case from a series of drug murders into a spectacle. And when Partardo reached trial, he did something almost no defendant does. He did not deny the killings. He embraced them. He took the stand and declared that he was a soldier in a war against drug dealers, that his victims deserve to die, and that he felt no remorse. He asked the jury not for mercy, but for validation. He wanted to be seen as an executioner of the guilty rather than a murderer of human beings. The jury did not accept his framing. In 1988, he was convicted on nine counts of firstdegree murder and sentenced to death. Investigators and prosecutors had built the case carefully, matching victims to evidence and dismantling the vigilante narrative piece by piece, showing that his choices had far more to do with self-interest and cruelty than with any coherent crusade. For decades, Partardo sat on Florida's death row, and he never abandoned his story. He continued to insist he had done right. In December of 2012, more than 24 years after his conviction, the state of Florida executed him by lethal injection. He was reportedly composed at the end, still the man who had graduated at the top of his class, still certain in his own logic to the last. What the case left behind was an uncomfortable reflection on the space between authority and vigilantism. Partardo had been trained to uphold the law and had come to believe that his training entitled him to replace it. The badge had shaped how he saw the world, and when the badge was gone, the sense of entitlement remained. Miami had seen no shortage of killers in those years. Few of them had once worn a uniform and stood at the front of their class, believing to the end that the law they had sworn to serve simply had not been ruthless enough. Number three, Joseph James D'Angelo. For decades, the investigators chasing the man they called the East Area Rapist and later the Golden State Killer were haunted by the same maddening quality in their suspect. He seemed to know how they worked. He was too careful. He moved through neighborhoods as though he had studied them, disabled outdoor lights, learned the routines of his victims, and vanished before patrols could close in. He seemed to think like a policeman. That intuition sat in the case files for 40 years, unproven and unshakable, and it turned out to be exactly correct. The man they were hunting had, for a time been one of them. The collision between the hunters and the hunted in this case took nearly half a century to complete, and when it did, it rewrote what investigators believed was possible in a cold case. But to understand the ending, you have to go back to the beginning to a man whose ordinariness was itself part of his camouflage. Joseph James D'Angelo was born in November of 1945. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam era and later studied criminal justice. In the early 1970s, he became a police officer, working first in Exit, California, and later in Auburn. To the people who worked alongside him, he was unremarkable, a competent, if unmemorable, officer. But even in those years, in the towns where he wore a badge, a series of unsolved break-ins and disturbing crimes were beginning that would later be linked through decades of investigative work to the same offender. His police career ended in 1979 when he was caught shoplifting a can of dog repellent and a hammer from a store. He was fired. On its surface, it was a petty, almost absurd end to a law enforcement career. But investigators would later see it differently. The dog repellent and the tools were the kind of items an intruder might use. And with his official access to authority gone, the crimes attributed to him did not stop. They escalated. Across the mid to late 1970s and into the 1980s, a single offender terrorized communities from the Sacramento region down through Southern California. He committed dozens of sexual assaults and a series of murders, moving between jurisdictions in a way that kept police departments from realizing for years that they were all chasing the same man. He was methodical to a degree that frustrated every task force assigned to him. He scouted homes in advance. He entered when he had studied the occupants. He left little that could identify him. In an era before DNA analysis matured, he was very nearly the perfect ghost. The turning point in the investigation was not a witness or a confession. It was science and patience. Investigators had preserved biological evidence from the crimes across all those years. As DNA technology advanced, they were able to establish that a long string of assaults and murders across the state had been committed by one person. But knowing there was one man was not the same as knowing who he was. His DNA matched no one in any criminal database. He had never been caught for the crimes that would have entered his profile into the system. The breakthrough came through a technique that would go on to transform cold case work everywhere. Investigators uploaded the killer's genetic profile to a public genealogy database, the kind ordinary people use to find distant relatives. They did not find the killer himself. They found his family tree. By working through that tree, narrowing down branches by age, location, and other details, they arrived at a single name, a retired man living quietly in a Sacramento suburb, a former police officer named Joseph D'Angelo. To confirm it, investigators quietly recovered a sample of his DNA from items he had discarded. It matched. In April of 2018, more than 40 years after the crimes began, D'Angelo was arrested. The man who had eluded an entire generation of detectives was an elderly retiree unremarkable to his neighbors. In 2020, he pleaded guilty to 13 murders and admitted to numerous kidnappings and rapes as part of an agreement that spared him the death penalty. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The near misses in his case were almost too painful to catalog. He had been a police officer during some of the earliest crimes. He had lived openly for decades. Any number of moments might have caught him sooner, and none did, because the technology that finally exposed him did not yet exist. What ended his freedom was not a mistake he made, but a scientific method that reached backward across 40 years to close a door he thought had long since sealed shut. His case changed the landscape of criminal investigation. Genetic genealogy, the technique that found him, has since been used to solve dozens of long, dormant cases. The former officer who had once seemed to think like a policeman was undone. In the end, by investigators who learned to think in ways no policeman ever had before, number four, Miky Popkov, the detectives in the Siberian city of Angars, spent years confronting a pattern of killings that carried a chilling professional quality. Women were being found in wooded areas on the outskirts of the city, and the crime scene suggested someone who understood how investigations were conducted. Someone who knew how to avoid leaving the traces that catch ordinary offenders. The victims often had one thing in common in their final hours. They had been out late, sometimes stranded, and had accepted a ride from a car that seemed safe. In a city where trust in a passing vehicle could be the difference between reaching home and vanishing, the killer had found the perfect disguise. And it took investigators far too long to see it. The man they were looking for was hiding inside the very institution meant to protect the city. And when the truth finally emerged, it forced Russian investigators to confront how a serial killer had operated for the better part of two decades under the cover of a police uniform. Miky Popkov worked as a patrol officer in Angars during the years his crimes were active. To his colleagues and to his own family, he presented himself as an ordinary man, married, employed, unremarkable. But according to the case later assembled against him, beginning in the early 1990s, he began attacking and killing women, and he continued to do so for nearly 20 years. Investigators came to understand that his position gave him extraordinary advantages. A police officer offering a woman a ride late at night was to most people the safest possible outcome. His uniform and his official vehicle dissolved the natural caution that might otherwise have saved lives. For years, the Angar's killings frustrated every effort to solve them. The sheer number of victims spread over a long period, and the killer's apparent familiarity with investigative methods kept the case cold. Some within the investigation reportedly suspected early on that they might be dealing with someone connected to law enforcement. precisely because the offender seemed to anticipate their every move. But suspicion is not evidence, and for a long time the case remained a wall investigators could not climb. The breakthrough came, as it did in other cases of this era, through advances in forensic analysis, combined with old-fashioned methodical elimination. Investigators undertook an enormous effort to test and compare biological and physical evidence against large numbers of men who had access to vehicles and who had been in the relevant areas during the relevant years. That painstaking work eventually narrowed toward Popcov. When the forensic links were established and he was confronted, the man who had hidden for so long began to talk. What he described stunned even experienced investigators. He confessed to killing not a handful of women, but dozens, a total that would place him among the most prolific killers ever documented in Russia. He offered explanations rooted in his own resentments and distorted beliefs about the women he targeted. A self-justifying narrative that investigators recognized as the familiar architecture of a man rationalizing monstrous acts. The cold precision of the crimes was mirrored in the cold detachment of his confessions. He was brought to trial and in 2015 convicted of the murders of 22 women and sentenced to life imprisonment. But the case did not end there. Investigators continued to work through the enormous backlog of unsolved killings that fit his pattern and Popcov continued to confess. In a second trial concluded in late 2018, he was found guilty of dozens more murders and received a second life sentence. The total number of his confirmed and confessed victims climbed into the range that made him by any measure one of the deadliest serial killers his country had ever prosecuted. The near misses in his case were structural rather than individual. There was no single overlooked clue that would have caught him early. Instead, there was a system in which a uniformed officer was almost by definition above the suspicion of ordinary citizens and in which the technology needed to link the crimes took years to mature. Every woman who accepted a ride from him did so for a reason that should have been sound. That was the horror of it. He had weaponized the very trust that his profession was supposed to earn. His exposure sent a shock through Russian law enforcement about how thoroughly a predator could exploit the authority of a badge. The Angar's killings had haunted the region for a generation, and the revelation that the killer had been a patrol officer the entire time was for many the hardest part to absorb. He remains imprisoned and investigators have continued even after his sentencing to examine whether the full scope of what he did has truly been accounted for. Number five, Antonet Frank. When New Orleans police arrived at the Kimon restaurant in the early hours of a March morning in 1995, they found a scene that made no immediate sense to the officers processing it. Three people had been shot. One of them was a fellow New Orleans police officer, an offduty man who had been working security. There was a survivor hiding in the restaurant, terrified. And when that survivor began to describe what had happened, the responding officers realized they were looking at something almost unthinkable. The person who had committed the murders was not a stranger. She was one of them. She was a New Orleans police officer who knew this restaurant, knew the family that ran it, and had worked security there herself. The speed with which this case was solved is what sets it apart from the others. There was no long manhunt, no cold decades. The collision between the killer and the investigators happened almost immediately because the survivor could name her. But the shock of it, an active duty officer walking back into a building she had just turned into a crime scene, is what made it unforgettable. And understanding how a person reached that point requires looking at the troubled path of Antwanet Frank. Frank was born in 1971 and joined the New Orleans Police Department in the early 1990s during a period when the department was under intense scrutiny for corruption and lacks hiring standards. Questions were later raised about how she had been admitted at all given concerns flagged during her application process, but she was hired, given a badge and a gun, and put on the street. Like many officers, she took on off-duty security work to supplement her income. And one of the places she worked was the Kim An restaurant, run by the VU family, who came to know and trust her. Alongside her official life, Frank had fallen in with an 18-year-old named Rogers Leay, and the two of them planned to rob the restaurant she was supposed to be guarding. On the night of the murders, they entered the building. Also present was Ronald Williams, an off-duty New Orleans officer working security, along with members of the VU family and their employees. During the robbery, Williams was shot and killed. Two young restaurant workers, Ha and Kuang, were also killed. It was a betrayal of the most fundamental kind. An officer turning her weapon on a fellow officer and on the very family that had welcomed her. What Frank apparently did not know was that two members of the family had managed to hide during the attack and had survived. One of them had seen enough to identify her and in a detail that investigators found almost impossible to believe. Frank returned to the restaurant afterward in her capacity as a police officer, as though responding to the crime, perhaps hoping to control the scene or account for her presence. Instead, she walked into the aftermath of her own crime while a survivor who could name her was still there. The case against her came together with unusual speed because of that survivor's testimony combined with the physical evidence and the accounts of what had happened inside. Leesay was arrested as well. The investigation that followed painted a portrait of an officer who had crossed every line her badge was supposed to represent. There was little of the slow forensic unraveling that marks other cases. The evidence pointed directly and immediately at a member of the force. Frank was tried and convicted of three counts of murder. In 1995, she was sentenced to death, becoming one of the very few women on Louisiana's death row and one of the only active police officers in the state's history to be condemned for such crimes. There was a further disturbing development after her sentencing when human remains were discovered buried beneath a property connected to her, raising additional questions that investigators pursued, but that never resulted in further charges of the same magnitude. Her case became a symbol of institutional failure. The concerns that had been raised during her hiring and the broader problems within the New Orleans Police Department of that era were held up as evidence of what could happen when the standards guarding the badge broke down. Here was a person who should never have been given the authority she was given and who used that authority to commit murder against her own colleague and against people who had trusted her. In the decades since, Frank has remained incarcerated as her case has moved through appeals and legal challenges over her sentence. The core facts have never been in serious doubt. What lingers is the institutional lesson that the failures which allowed her to wear a badge were in a real sense part of the chain of events that led three people to die in a restaurant that had considered her a friend. Number six, Len Davis. Federal agents in New Orleans in 1994 were running a surveillance operation on police corruption, wiring conversations, and listening to the daily communications of officers suspected of protecting drug operations. What they captured on their recordings turned an ordinary corruption case into something far darker. They heard an officer arranging in real time the murder of a woman. And then in the hours that followed, they heard him waiting for confirmation that she was dead. The chilling reality was that the very wiretap meant to document bribery instead documented a killing as it was being ordered, and the investigators listening were, for a terrible stretch of time, unable to stop it. That is the anguish at the center of this case. The near miss that was not a near miss at all, but a catastrophe overheard. To understand how it happened, you have to look at Len Davis, an officer whose reputation on the streets of New Orleans had become a kind of dark legend. Davis was born in 1964 and served as an officer in the New Orleans Police Department. In the Desire Housing Development, where he worked, he had reportedly earned the nickname Robocop, a name that captured both the fear he inspired and the aggressive style of policing he was known for. He was, by the accounts that emerged, an officer who had come to see himself as beyond accountability, operating with a sense of impunity in the communities he was supposed to serve. In October of 1994, a woman named Kim Groves witnessed Davis, or an associate, involved in an act of brutality against a young man in her neighborhood. She did what citizens are supposed to do. She filed a complaint against the officer. It was a lawful ordinary exercise of the right to hold police accountable. To Davis, according to the case later proven against him, it was an unforgivable offense. Here, the federal investigation and Davis's own actions intersected in a way that would define the case. Unknown to Davis, his communications were being monitored as part of a broader corruption probe. Agents listened as he learned of the complaint and as he set in motion a plan to have Groves killed. He enlisted an accomplice to carry out the shooting. The recordings captured his coordination of the crime, his impatience, and finally his reaction upon learning that Groves had been shot and killed outside her home. She was 32 years old and a mother. The investigators who heard these communications faced an agonizing situation. The nature of surveillance operations and the speed at which events unfolded created a window in which a murder was set in motion faster than it could be prevented. That failure to intervene in time became one of the most painful aspects of the entire case. A reminder of the gap that can exist between hearing that something terrible is about to happen and being able to stop it. But the recordings that could not save Kim Groves became the instrument of justice against the man who ordered her death. The federal government brought charges against Davis for violating Groves's civil rights through murder. A federal framework used when a person acting under the authority of the state deprivives someone of their rights. In this case, the ultimate deprivation. The evidence was overwhelming because Davis had in effect narrated his own crime into a federal recording. He was convicted and the case moved through the federal death penalty process. For years, Davis remained under a federal death sentence. His case tangled in appeals over the conduct of the proceedings and the appropriateness of the punishment. The core facts were never seriously disputed. An officer had ordered the murder of a citizen for the act of filing a complaint against him, and federal investigators had captured it happening. In a significant development, Davis's death sentence was later commuted as part of broader federal clemency actions, converting his punishment to imprisonment rather than execution, though he remained incarcerated for the crime. The commutation did nothing to change what he had done, and it reopened old wounds for the family of Kim Groves, who had lived for decades with the knowledge of how she died and why. The case stands as one of the starkkest examples of the abuse of police authority in modern American history. Kim Groves had exercised a basic democratic right, the right to hold power accountable, and an officer had answered that with a contract on her life. The recordings that documented it ensured that Davis could never escape responsibility, even as they preserved forever the sound of a crime that investigators heard but could not prevent. Number seven, Anthony Jack Sully. Detectives in the San Francisco Bay area in 1983 were confronted with a string of disappearances and murders that seemed at first to have no common thread. The victims came from different corners of the region's underworld and its margins. People connected to drugs, to the sex trade, to money that moved through channels the police could not easily trace. As the bodies were discovered, investigators began to sense that a single hand was behind them, someone organized and ruthless. What they did not initially grasp was that the man responsible had once carried a badge in one of their own neighboring departments and had brought a lawman's understanding of investigation to the concealment of his crimes. The dual nature of this case, a former officer using what he had learned as police to evade police is what gives it its unsettling character. Piecing it together meant tracing the collapse of Anthony Sully, a man whose life had followed a steep and destructive arc from public service into addiction and murder. Sully was born in 1944 and had served as a police officer in Milbre, a community on the San Francisco Peninsula. For a time, he was by outward measures a functioning member of law enforcement. But his life unraveled through drug use. And as his addiction deepened, he descended into the very criminal world he had once been sworn to police. By the early 1980s, the former officer was inshed in drugs and the desperate, violent economics that surrounded them. Over a period of roughly 6 months in 1982 and 1983, Sully committed a series of murders that would ultimately number six victims. The killings were tied to the drug trade and to Sully's increasingly volatile and predatory behavior. He used a warehouse space as the site for some of his crimes, a location that would later become central to the evidence against him. The victims included both men and women drawn from the circles in which he now moved. The investigation that closed in on him relied on the accumulation of physical evidence and the connections between the victims and Sully's operation. His warehouse, when it was searched, yielded evidence that tied him directly to the killings. Whatever advantages his police training might have given him in concealment, they were not enough to overcome the sheer volume of what he had done and the traces it left behind. The bodies, the location, and the links between them formed a chain that led investigators to his door. The irony was not lost on anyone involved. A man who had once been trained to gather evidence and solve crimes had become the subject of exactly that process, and the skills he might have used to hide were outmatched by the methodical work of the detectives assigned to the case. His former profession may have shaped how he tried to avoid detection, but it did not save him from it. Sully was arrested, tried, and in 1986 convicted of multiple counts of murder. He was sentenced to death and sent to San Quentin, joining the ranks of California's condemned. There he would remain for the rest of his life, his case moving through the endless machinery of appeals that characterizes the state's death penalty system. Unlike some killers who court publicity, Sully spent his decades on death row in relative obscurity, though he became the subject of long correspondence and study by those interested in understanding how a person crosses from the enforcement of law into its most extreme violation. In September of 2023, after nearly four decades on death row, Sully died of natural causes at a medical facility associated with San Quentin. He was 79 years old, and his death closed a case that had never been in serious doubt, but that had lingered for the better part of 40 years. The lasting significance of Sully's story lies in what it reveals about dcent. He was not born a killer, at least not in any way. The record shows he had been a police officer entrusted with the community safety, and drugs and violence had hollowed that out until nothing recognizable remained. The warehouse in which he committed his crimes became a symbol of how completely a life could invert. A former guardian of order turning a building into a place of murder and being caught in the end by the same investigative process he had once been paid to carry out. Number eight, David Middleton. The investigators in Reno, Nevada in early 1995 were working the murder of a local school teacher, and one piece of evidence troubled them more than any other. The killing showed signs of planning and restraint that did not fit an impulsive crime. There were indications that the victim had been held and controlled before her death, that the perpetrator had understood how to move a body and manage a scene, that this was someone who had thought carefully about not getting caught. As they built the case, detectives kept circling back to that quality of professionalism, and it led them eventually to a man whose easygoing manner as a cable installer concealed a past in law enforcement, and a mind that had turned that training toward predation. The tension in this case comes from the gap between how David Middleton appeared and what he was doing behind the friendly exterior. He was the man who came to fix your cable, personable and unremarkable, and understanding how that man became a killer required investigators to look back at a life that had already contained warning signs. Middleton was born in June of 1961 and had worked as a police officer in Miami, Florida earlier in his life. His time in law enforcement gave him knowledge of how crimes were investigated and how evidence was gathered. knowledge that in the wrong mind becomes a blueprint for avoiding detection. His life eventually took him to the Reno area where he worked as a cable television installer. A job that gave him access to homes and to the routines of the people who lived in them. The nickname that would later attach to him, the cable guy, captured the ordinary, trusted role he occupied in the community. The crimes that brought him down involved two women. One was Katherine Powell, an elementary school teacher in the Reno area. The other was Thelma Davila, a casino worker. The investigation revealed that Middleton had abducted and controlled his victims using a storage shed he maintained as a site connected to his crimes. The details established at trial showed a level of premeditation that reflected his understanding of how to avoid leaving the traces that catch most offenders. The investigation closed in on him through the connections between the victims and the physical evidence and crucially through the storage facility he rented. Investigators established a timeline linking his movements to the crimes, including his visits to the shed around the times relevant to the murders. His former police training may have made him more careful than the average offender, but it could not erase the accumulated weight of the evidence. The very care he took became, in a sense, part of the profile that pointed to someone with specialized knowledge. When the case reached trial, the evidence against Middleton included the forensic links, the timeline, and the account of how the crimes had been committed. He was convicted of murder in connection with both women. Jurors found multiple aggravating circumstances that justified the harshest available punishment, including his prior record and the calculated nature of the killings. He was sentenced to death. His case moved through the Nevada courts on appeal over the following years, and the death sentence was upheld by the state's higher courts, which examined and rejected his challenges to the aggravating factors and the conduct of his trial. The judicial record steadily affirmed what the investigators had established, that this was a man who had used the trust of an ordinary job and the knowledge of a former profession to commit deliberate murder. Investigators long suspected that Middleton might be connected to other crimes beyond the two for which he was convicted, given the methodical nature of what he had done and the mobility his life had afforded him. Those suspicions, like similar ones in other cases of this kind, could not all be resolved with the certainty required for prosecution, and they remain part of the shadow the case casts. The story of David Middleton endures as a study in concealment. The former officer turned cable installer had built a life that made him welcome in homes and invisible in the community. And he had layered onto that ordinariness the specialized knowledge of a man who had once investigated crime himself. When the two women he killed were finally connected to him, it was through the same patient investigative work he had once been trained to perform the profession he had abandoned reaching forward to hold him accountable for the way he had betrayed it. Number nine, Louisie Epalito. When federal prosecutors in the early 2000s finally moved against two retired New York City detectives, the accusation was so extreme that many people struggled to believe it. These were not officers accused of taking bribes or looking the other way. They were accused of having worked while wearing the badge as murderers for the mob, using their access to police files and their authority as detectives to help the Lucosi crime family identify, locate, and kill its enemies. For years, the rumors had circulated in law enforcement and organized crime circles, dismissed by many as too outrageous to be true. The investigation that proved them real would expose one of the deepest betrayals in the history of American policing. The unraveling of Louis Epileto centered on the collision between a decorated detective's public image and the secret role he and his partner had played, and it began in part with the very organized crime world they had served turning against them. Epilito was a New York City detective who cultivated a colorful public persona. He came from a family with documented ties to organized crime, a background he did not hide and even discussed openly, and he later wrote about his life in law enforcement. To much of the public, he appeared as a tough, street-wise cop. But according to the federal case built against him and his partner Steven Carakappa, that image concealed a criminal enterprise operating from within the department itself. Between roughly 1986 and 1990, Epilito and Carakappa functioned as covert assets for the Luché family and specifically for a powerful figure within it. In exchange for money, they allegedly provided confidential law enforcement information. the locations of targets, the identities of informants, the status of investigations. In several cases, the assistants went beyond information. The detectives were implicated in facilitating and even directly participating in murders, using their badges to stop targets, to gain access or to deliver victims to their killers. The total number of homicides connected to their conduct reached eight, a staggering figure for men sworn to prevent exactly such crimes. For years, these activities remained hidden. The two men retired from the NYPD and relocated, and the rumors trailed behind them without ever hardening into charges. What eventually brought the case forward was the cooperation of organized crime figures who described the detective's role, combined with the persistent work of investigators who assembled testimony, financial connections, and the pattern of information that had flowed from inside the department to the mob. When the case finally came together, the arrests made outside a restaurant ended two decades of speculation. The subsequent trial laid out the extraordinary allegation in detail that two detectives had for money betrayed not only their oath but the fundamental purpose of their profession, turning the tools of law enforcement into instruments of murder for hire. In 2006, a federal jury convicted Epileto and Caracappa on charges connected to their role in the murders and the broader criminal enterprise. The case then entered a period of legal complexity with disputes over statutes of limitations and the framing of the charges that led to appeals and delays. Ultimately, the convictions were sustained and both men received sentences of life imprisonment, ending any possibility that they would walk free. The near misses in this case were measured in years. The detectives had operated during the height of their activity without being caught, had retired comfortably, and had very nearly aged out of accountability entirely. The mob world they served was in the end part of what exposed them, as cooperating witnesses from that world provided the testimony that investigators needed. The men who had used the badge to serve killers were undone in part by the killers themselves. The case sent a profound shock through the New York City Police Department and the public. It represented a nightmare scenario, not corruption at the margins, but the complete capture of law enforcement authority by organized crime with detectives serving as executioners. Both men would die in custody, but the damage to public trust, the sense that the line between the police and the criminals had been not just crossed, but erased, endured long after the verdicts. The story of the mafia cops became a permanent cautionary tale about how deep betrayal can run when those with power decide to sell it. Number 10, Roger Kibby. For years, the investigators along the Interstate 5 corridor in Northern California worked a series of murders that shared a distinctive and deliberate signature. Young women had been found in remote areas near the highways around Sacramento, and the way the killer handled his victims. The specific cuts he made to their clothing, the methodical nature of the crimes, pointed to a single offender with a fixed and disturbing set of behaviors. They gave him a name, the I-5 Strangler, and for a long time that name was all they had. The man behind it was quiet, unremarkable, and skilled at leaving little behind, and the case would take years and a stroke of forensic progress to close. The pursuit of Roger Kibby was a long procedural grind, and the moments when he nearly slipped away entirely are what make the case a study in the patience required to catch a careful killer. Understanding him meant looking at a man whose outward life gave almost no hint of what he was doing on the roads at night. Kibby was born in May of 1939. He lived a largely ordinary working life, holding various jobs over the years, including work that touched on security and manual trades. To those around him he was withdrawn and unremarkable, the kind of man who drew little attention. That quality of blending in was central to how he operated. He found his victims along the freeways, often young women who were traveling or in vulnerable circumstances, and he used the anonymity of the highway corridors to approach them and to dispose of evidence far from where he might be recognized. The killings attributed to him occurred across roughly a decade from the late 1970s into the late 1980s. Investigators recognized the pattern, the connection to the I5 corridor and other freeways, the particular way the victims were treated, the signs of a killer acting out a specific and repeated compulsion. But recognizing a pattern is not the same as identifying a man, and for years, the case remained frustratingly open, a series of connected crimes without a face. The turning point came in 1987 when Kibby was linked to the murder of a young woman named Darcy Frackenpole. Physical evidence in that case, including trace materials and the specific characteristics that matched the I-5 pattern, allowed investigators to build a case against him. Forensic analysis of fibers and other evidence tied him to the crime in a way that the earlier killings with their thinner evidentiary trails had not permitted. It was the careful work of connecting microscopic traces to a specific suspect that finally gave the I5 strangler a name. Kibby was prosecuted and in 1991 he was convicted in connection with the Fracken Pole murder and sentenced to a term of imprisonment. But investigators believed he was responsible for more deaths than that single conviction reflected, and they did not consider the case truly finished. Over the years that followed, as forensic technology continued to advance, cold case detectives returned to the older I-5 killings with new tools. That renewed effort paid off. Advances in DNA analysis eventually allowed investigators to connect Kibby conclusively to additional murders from the earlier years of the pattern. Confronted with this evidence and by then already imprisoned, Kibby entered into an arrangement in which he acknowledged responsibility for a series of additional killings in exchange for a sentence that kept him behind bars for life. The full scope of the I5 Strangler's crimes, long suspected, was finally established through the persistence of investigators who had refused to let the older cases die. The near misses in Kibby's story were the years themselves. The long stretch during which he continued to operate because the evidence needed to catch him did not yet exist in usable form. Each advance in forensic science pulled the truth a little closer until at last the technology caught up with the crimes. Kibby spent the remainder of his life in prison. In February of 2021, at the age of 81, he was killed by another inmate inside Mule Creek State Prison, strangled in his cell in a grim echo of the method he had used against his own victims. His death closed the book on a man who had haunted the California freeways for a decade and whose full accounting had required the better part of a lifetime of investigative work to complete. The I5 corridor, once a hunting ground, had long since given up its secret, but only because the detectives who worked it refused to accept that a careful killer could stay hidden forever. Number 11, Charles Becker. In the summer of 1912, a gambler named Herman Rosenthal was shot dead on a Manhattan street, and the New York City press seized on the killing with an intensity that would shape the case from the start. What made the murder extraordinary was not the death of a gambler, which was common enough in that era, but the identity of the man who would soon stand accused of arranging it. He was a police lieutenant, the commander of a squad tasked with cracking down on illegal gambling, and Rosenthal had been on the verge of publicly exposing his corruption. The investigators and prosecutors who took up the case were about to put a serving police official on trial for murder, something the city had never seen, and the political machinery of the age would twist around the proceedings at every turn. The story of Charles Becker unfolds against the backdrop of Tamonn Hall, New York. A world where the line between the police and the criminals they policed was often deliberately blurred and where a man in Becker's position could grow rich from the very vice he was supposed to suppress. Becker was a longtime member of the New York City Police Department who had risen to the rank of lieutenant. By 1911, he had been placed in charge of a so-called strong arms squad, ostensibly dedicated to enforcing the laws against gambling. In practice, according to the case that emerged, the position was an engine of extortion. Gambling operations in the city paid for protection, and an officer positioned as Becker was could extract enormous sums by choosing whom to raid and whom to leave alone. Herman Rosenthal was a gambling operator who had at one point been connected to Becker's arrangements. Their relationship soured and Rosenthal began to talk. He went to the press and to the district attorney preparing to expose the corruption that ran through the police department's gambling enforcement. With Becker at its center, Rosenthal's testimony threatened to bring down not just Becker, but the wider system of graft. And before he could deliver the most damaging of it, he was gunned down outside a Manhattan hotel by a group of gunmen associated with the city's criminal underworld, the investigation moved quickly, driven by public outrage and pressure. The gunmen were identified and apprehended, and the prosecution's theory was that they had been hired to kill Rosenthal at Becker's direction to silence the man who threatened to destroy him. The case against Becker rested heavily on the testimony of intermediaries and associate who connected the lieutenant to the arrangement of the murder. Testimony that would later be the subject of intense dispute. Becker was tried and convicted of orchestrating the murder. But the case was so entangled with the politics and the sensational press coverage of the era that it did not rest easily. Questions were raised about the reliability of the witnesses. some of whom had strong incentives to implicate Becker in exchange for leniency and about whether the proceedings had been fair. His conviction was overturned on appeal and he was tried a second time. Again he was convicted. The gunman who carried out the shooting were executed and in July of 1915 after his appeals were exhausted. Charles Becker was put to death in the electric chair at Sing Singh Prison. He became the only New York City police officer ever executed for murder, a grim distinction that has held ever since. The case has remained a subject of historical debate for more than a century. Some who have studied it have questioned whether the evidence against Becker truly met the standard his ultimate punishment required given the compromised nature of the witnesses and the political forces arrayed against him. Others have concluded that he was indeed the corrupt architect the prosecution described. What is not in dispute is that Becker operated at the rotten heart of a system in which police power and criminal enterprise were deeply intertwined and that he grew rich from it. The lasting significance of the Becker case lies in what it exposed about that system. It pulled back the curtain on the machinery of police corruption in Tamony era New York on the protection rackets and the money that flowed between the underworld and the men in uniform. The execution of a police lieutenant sent a message, however imperfect, that even those at the center of that machinery could be brought down. And more than a hundred years later, the questions surrounding his guilt ensure that the case continues to be argued. A reminder that the collision between police corruption and justice is rarely as clean as anyone would wish. Number 12, John Regginald Halliday Christi. When the new tenants of a house at 10 Willington Place in London made a grim discovery behind a papered over kitchen wall in 1953, the investigators who responded uncovered a horror that had been hidden in plain sight for years. The bodies of several women were concealed within the property, and as the search widened, more remains were found buried in the small garden. The man who had lived there, a mild-mannered figure who had once served as a wartime police reservist and who was known to neighbors as quiet and respectable, had vanished. The manhunt that followed and the confessions that came with his capture would expose one of the most disturbing cases in British criminal history and would eventually force the nation to confront a terrible miscarriage of justice. The story of John Christie is one in which the trusted appearance of a man concealed a predator and in which the very ordinariness that made him seem harmless was the disguise that allowed him to kill for years without suspicion. Christy was born in April of 1899 in Halifax, England. He served in the First World War and carried into adulthood a personality that struck those around him as reserved and unremarkable. He had a criminal record for minor offenses earlier in life, but nothing that marked him as dangerous. During the Second World War, in a detail that lends the case its especially unsettling quality, Christy volunteered and served as a special constable, a wartime police reservist, giving him a measure of authority and the trust of his community during the years of the conflict. He and his wife lived at 10 Place, an unremarkable address in the Notting Hill area of London. It was there, over a period stretching from the 1940s into the early 1950s, that Christy carried out a series of murders. His victims were women, and the methods he used, established through the later investigation, and his own confessions, revealed a calculated and predatory nature entirely at odds with the meek figure his neighbors thought they knew. The case is inseparable from one of the most tragic errors in the history of British justice. Years before Christiey's crimes were discovered, another man, Timothy Evans, who had lived in the same building, was tried and executed for the murder of his own wife and infant daughter. Christy had been a witness against Evans. It was only after Christiey's own crimes came to light that the terrible possibility emerged, that Christy, not Evans, had been responsible for at least one of the deaths for which Evans had hanged. When Christy was finally arrested and began to confess, he admitted to a number of killings and in doing so cast a devastating shadow over the earlier conviction and execution of Evans. The investigation that closed in on Christy followed the discovery of the bodies at Willington Place. With the horror of the scene established a nationwide search was launched for the missing tenant. Christy was found and taken into custody and under questioning he confessed to murdering multiple women including his own wife. Ethel whose body was among those found in the house. Christy was tried for murder. His defense raised questions about his mental state but the jury convicted him. In July of 1953 he was hanged executed by the same hangman, Albert Pierre Point, who had earlier carried out the execution of Timothy Evans. A grim symmetry that only deepened the tragedy. The aftermath of the case reverberated through British society for years. The likelihood that Timothy Evans had been wrongly executed for a crime Christy committed became a central argument in the movement against capital punishment in the United Kingdom. Official inquiries examined the Evans conviction and Evans was eventually granted aostumous pardon. The case is widely credited as one of the significant factors that contributed to the eventual abolition of the death penalty in Britain precisely because it demonstrated in the starkkest possible terms that the system could execute an innocent man. The story of the man who had once been a special constable, who had held a small measure of the community's trust during wartime, and who had used the cover of his ordinary respectability to murder women in his own home, became one of the defining criminal cases of 20th century Britain. Its influence did not end with Christiey's execution. It reshaped the national conversation about justice, punishment, and the terrible cost of getting it wrong. Number 13, Steven Rios. The detectives in Columbia, Missouri, working the 2004 murder of a young college student named Jesse Valencia, were focused early on the physical evidence found at the scene, and one piece of it would eventually break the case wide open. Hairs recovered from the victim's body did not belong to him. When those hairs were analyzed and compared, they matched a man who had inserted himself into the investigation in a way that should have been impossible for an innocent person. A police officer who had denied any recent contact with the victim, yet whose own hair had been left on the body. The investigation that followed would peel back the double life of Steven Rios and reveal a killing committed to protect a secret. The tension in this case lies in the collapse of an officer's carefully maintained public and private facade and in the way the smallest trace of physical evidence contradicted the story he told. Rios was a police officer in Colombia, a married man with a young child and an outwardly conventional life. Behind that public face, according to the case established at trial, he had been involved in a secret relationship with Jesse Valencia, a young man who was a student in the community. When that relationship threatened to become known, it created exactly the kind of pressure that, the prosecution argued drove Rios to murder in order to keep his double life from unraveling. Jess Valencia was found dead in the summer of 2004. His death the result of violence that indicated a personal and close attack rather than a random one. As detectives worked the case, they examined the people who had been connected to the young man and Rios's name surfaced. The officer maintained that he had not had recent contact with Valencia, distancing himself from any current involvement. But the forensic evidence told a different story. The hairs found on the victim's body were the crux of the case. Analysis linked them to Rios, directly contradicting his account of having had no recent contact. Prosecutors argued that the physical evidence, combined with the established relationship and the motive to conceal it, pointed to Rios as the killer. The theory advanced at trial was that Rios had used his knowledge and physical training as a police officer in the commission of the crime. a chilling inversion of the skills he had been given to protect the public. The case moved through the courts in a way that reflected its complexity. Rios was convicted of murder in an initial trial in 2004. That conviction, however, was later overturned on appeal due to issues with the proceedings and the case was sent back for a new trial. This is the kind of turn that can unravel a prosecution entirely and it placed enormous weight on the strength of the underlying evidence. At the retrial in December of 2008, the case against Rios held. He was again convicted, this time of secondderee murder along with an additional charge and he was sentenced to life imprisonment. The appellet courts subsequently upheld this outcome, affirming that the evidence, particularly the forensic link that had contradicted his account, was sufficient to sustain the conviction. The Rios case became a widely studied example of an officer whose crime grew out of the desperate effort to protect a hidden life. Unlike the serial predators and organized killers found elsewhere among these cases, Rios was a man whose single terrible act was driven by the fear of exposure. The badge he carried did not create the impulse to kill, but the prosecution argued it shaped the way he carried it out, and the confidence with which he believed he could deflect suspicion. What the case ultimately demonstrated was the power of small physical evidence to override the word of a person in authority. Rios had counted, it seemed, on his position and his denials to insulate him. Instead, a handful of hairs trace evidence of a kind that an officer of all people should have understood, placed him in contact with the victim he claimed not to have seen. The investigators who worked the case did not need a confession or an eyewitness. They needed only the truth that the physical world had preserved, and it was enough to hold a police officer accountable for murder. Number 14, Drew Peterson. The suspicion that eventually surrounded Drew Peterson, a police sergeant in Bowling Brook, Illinois, did not begin with a body or a crime scene. It began with a disappearance. In late October of 2007, his fourth wife, a 23-year-old woman, vanished without a trace. As investigators and the public focused on the missing woman, attention turned to something that had been quietly closed years earlier, the death of Peterson's third wife, Kathleen Savio, whose body had been found in a dry bathtub in 2004 and whose death had been ruled an accident. The disappearance of one wife caused authorities to re-examine the death of another. And what they found would lead to a murder conviction against a man who, as a police officer, understood exactly how investigations worked. The unsettling core of this case is that the suspect was a veteran law enforcement officer, someone who knew the procedures, the evidence, and the pitfalls, and who very nearly benefited from a death that had already been officially explained away. Peterson had spent decades as a police officer in Bowlingbrook, rising to the rank of sergeant. His personal life was marked by a series of marriages, and it was the intersection of two of them that would define his legacy. In 2004, Kathleen Savio, from whom he was in the process of finalizing a divorce, was found dead in her bathtub. At the time, her death was ruled an accidental drowning. There was suspicion in some quarters. Even then, given the circumstances and the contentious nature of the divorce, but no charges were brought, and the case was closed. 3 years later, in 2007, Peterson's fourth wife disappeared. Her family and friends did not believe she had left voluntarily, and the case drew intense public and media attention. As investigators dug into Peterson's history, the earlier death of Kathleen Savio took on a new and sinister significance. Authorities made the decision to exume Savio's body and conduct a new examination. The re-examination reached a starkly different conclusion from the original finding. Forensic analysis of Sevilla's injuries and the circumstances of her death led experts to determine that it had not been an accident at all, but a homicide. The injuries were more consistent with an attack than with an accidental fall in the bathtub. With that reclassification, the case that had been closed for years was reopened as a murder investigation, and Peterson became its central figure. The prosecution that followed was legally complex and in some respects groundbreaking. Because the case relied in part on statements from people who were no longer available to testify, including Savio herself and Peterson's missing fourth wife, prosecutors used and helped shape legal provisions allowing certain hearsay statements to be admitted when a defendant is believed to have made a witness unavailable. This framework developed and applied in the Illinois proceedings became a notable aspect of the case's legal significance. In 2012, Drew Peterson was convicted of the firstdegree murder of Kathleen Savio. The following year, he was sentenced to 38 years in prison. His conviction was subsequently upheld through the appellet process, including affirmation by the Illinois Supreme Court, which reviewed and rejected his challenges to the proceedings. The disappearance of his fourth wife, which had triggered the re-examination of Savio's death, was never resolved with a body or a separate conviction. She remains missing, and Peterson has consistently denied any involvement in her disappearance. The mystery of what happened to her lingers as an open wound alongside the conviction for the murder he was ultimately found to have committed. The Peterson case captured national attention in part because of the audacity it seemed to represent. A police officer suspected of killing a wife and having the death written off as an accident only to be undone when a second wife's disappearance forced everyone to look again. It became a cautionary example of how an initial investigation can miss what a later, more skeptical examination reveals, and of how a person's knowledge of law enforcement can be turned toward evading it. In the end, the very scrutiny that Peterson understood so well was what closed in on him, reaching back to reopen a case that had, for a time, been left for dead. Number 15, Steven Carakappa. The full weight of the mafia cops case did not fall only on the more flamboyant of the two detectives. Investigators who worked to expose the conspiracy came to understand that the quieter partner Steven Caracappa was in some ways the more chilling figure, a decorated detective who had served on units dedicated to investigating organized crime and homicide and who had used that very position to feed information to the killers he was supposed to be pursuing. The final entry in this record belongs to him because his story illustrates how the betrayal ran through even the most trusted corners of the department and how long it took for the truth to be proven. Where his partner cultivated attention, Kakappa was known within the department as reserved and professional, which made the revelation of his conduct all the more disturbing to those who had worked alongside him. Caracappa was a New York City police detective who built a respected career including service connected to major case and organized crime investigative work. That assignment placed him in a position of extraordinary trust with access to sensitive information about investigations into the very crime families that he and his partner Lewis Epileto would come to serve. According to the federal case, this access was precisely what made him so valuable to the Luchese organization. He could learn who was cooperating with law enforcement, who was under investigation, and where targets could be found. Between roughly 1986 and 1990, Carakappa and Epilito operated as secret agents for the crime family, providing information and assistance that facilitated a series of murders. Caracappa's role, given his investigative position, was central to the flow of confidential law enforcement information into the hands of the mob. The eight murders connected to the two detectives conduct represented a catastrophic subversion of everything their work was supposed to stand for. Men who were paid to solve homicides were instead helping to arrange them. For years, the pair evaded detection. They completed their careers, retired and relocated, and the rumors that trailed them remained unproven. It was only through the eventual cooperation of organized crime figures, combined with the meticulous reconstruction of the information trail and the financial connections, that investigators were able to build a case capable of withstanding trial. The killers the detectives had served became, in the end, part of the evidence against them. When the case reached its conclusion, the two detectives were arrested together and their trial laid bare the full scope of the conspiracy. In 2006, a federal jury convicted Caracappa along with Epileto on charges tied to the murders and the criminal enterprise. As with his partner, the case then passed through a period of legal wrangling over technical issues, including the timing of the charges, which produced appeals and delays before the convictions were ultimately sustained. Caracappa was sentenced to life imprisonment. He would not leave custody. In 2017, he died in prison. His death closing the chapter on a detective who had risen through the ranks of one of the nation's most storied police departments only to become one of its greatest traitors. The near misses in his story were the long years of unproven rumor during which a former investigator lived freely despite the suspicions that surrounded him. What finally caught him was the patient assembly of evidence from the criminal world. he had served and the refusal of investigators to let the case fade simply because so much time had passed and because the accused had once worn the same badge. The lasting significance of Carakappa's part in the story is the reminder that betrayal is often quietest at its most dangerous. He did not draw attention to himself. He did his job or appeared to and used the trust that came with it to serve killers. When people speak of the line between the police and the criminals they pursue, this case stands as the moment that line was not merely crossed but obliterated by men who had been given every reason and every duty to protect it. His conviction and the life sentence that followed ensured that the erasure of that line carried a permanent cost. Across all 15 of these cases, from a Florida deputy who hunted along empty roads to New York detectives who sold their badges to the mob, a single uncomfortable truth runs beneath the surface. Each of these individuals was handed the trust of a community and the authority to enforce its laws. And each of them turned that trust into a weapon. The badge that was meant to protect became in their hands the very thing that allowed them to harm. What these stories share is not a single method or motive, but the betrayal at their core and the long patient work of the investigators who sometimes across decades refused to let that betrayal go unanswered.
fullTextVi: Số một, Gerard John Schaefer. Các thám tử ở Quận Martin, Florida, vào mùa hè năm 1972, đã phải đối mặt với một vấn đề không phù hợp với hình dạng thông thường của một tội phạm. Hai cô gái tuổi teen bước vào đồn cảnh sát, bị sốc nặng và kể lại một câu chuyện không có ý nghĩa trên giấy. Một người đàn ông mặc đồng phục, một người đàn ông đeo huy hiệu, một người đàn ông lẽ ra phải bảo vệ họ, đã chĩa súng đuổi họ vào đầm lầy, trói họ đến những cái cây và nói cho chúng biết anh ta định làm gì. Và rồi, vì lý do gì không ai giải thích được, anh nhận được một cuộc điện thoại hoảng sợ và để họ sống. Người đàn ông mà họ mô tả không phải là một người xa lạ ẩn nấp trong bóng tối. Ông ấy là phó cảnh sát trưởng. Anh ấy là một trong số họ. Sự mâu thuẫn đó là trung tâm của mọi chuyện diễn ra sau đó và các nhà điều tra sẽ chi nhiều năm cố gắng để hiểu nó. Làm thế nào mà một người tuyên thệ thi hành luật lại sử dụng chính luật đó như một công cụ săn bắn? Để trả lời điều đó, họ phải truy tìm cuộc đời của Gerrard John Schaefer. Và những gì họ tìm thấy là một mô hình đã tồn tại trong nhiều năm, nếu chỉ có ai đó biết nơi để tìm. Schaefer sinh vào tháng 3 năm 1946 tại Wisconsin và lớn lên trong một gia đình sau đó ông đã mô tả bằng những lời cay đắng. Bằng lời kể của chính mình nhiều năm sau đó, anh lớn lên trong sự oán giận với cha mình và tập trung vào em gái của mình, người mà anh tin rằng đã nhận được tình cảm của anh từ chối. Liệu sự oán giận đó có giải thích được điều gì hay không, là câu hỏi dành cho các nhà tâm lý học, không phải thám tử mà là các nhà điều tra sau này sẽ lưu ý rằng sự tức giận mà anh ta mang theo đối với phụ nữ xuất hiện sớm và không bao giờ bên trái. Khi còn trẻ, ông đã thử và thất bại trên nhiều con đường. Anh ta học làm linh mục và từ bỏ nó. Anh ta đã thử giảng dạy và được cho là đã bị sa thải sau những hành vi gây bất ổn xung quanh các học sinh nữ. Mỗi thất bại, thưa ông, dường như mài giũa điều gì đó trong ông hơn là làm nó mềm đi. Các đặc vụ đã lắng nghe khi anh ấy biết về khiếu nại và khi anh ấy bắt đầu hành động một kế hoạch giết Groves. Anh ta chiêu mộ một đồng phạm để thực hiện vụ nổ súng. Các nhà điều tra nghe được những thông tin liên lạc này đã phải đối mặt với một tình huống đau đớn. Bản chất của các hoạt động giám sát và tốc độ diễn ra các sự kiện đã tạo ra một cửa sổ trong đó một vụ giết người diễn ra nhanh hơn mức có thể bị ngăn chặn. Việc không can thiệp kịp thời đã trở thành một trong những khía cạnh đau đớn nhất của toàn bộ vụ án. Một lời nhắc nhở về khoảng cách có thể tồn tại giữa việc nghe được điều gì đó khủng khiếp là sắp xảy ra và có khả năng ngăn chặn nó. Nhưng những đoạn ghi âm không thể cứu được Kim Groves đã trở thành công cụ của công lý chống lại kẻ đã ra lệnh giết cô. Chính phủ liên bang đưa ra cáo buộc chống lại Davis vì vi phạm quyền công dân của Groves thông qua tội giết người. Bằng chứng rất rõ ràng vì trên thực tế, Davis đã thuật lại tội ác của chính mình vào một bản ghi âm liên bang. Anh ta bị kết án và vụ án được chuyển sang quy trình xử tử hình liên bang.
